Why experts are pushing RFK Jr. to release a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods
Health
Oct 23, 2026 4:24 PM EDT
Significant delays in the Trump administration's effort to tackle the health risks of ultraprocessed foods have obstructed a pillar of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" agenda and caused growing frustration inside and outside the government.
More than 100 science, medical and nutrition experts signed and sent an open letter Friday to the Office of Management and Budget, urging the administration to release the first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed foods (UPF).
"It is critical that special interests not hold up this process," the letter read. "Most Americans are aware of UPF and wish to avoid them, but deeper familiarity with UPF remains limited, signaling a need for guidance."
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
The Trump administration first announced their efforts to define ultraprocessed foods back in July 2025, but according to media reports, food company CEOs intervened in the definition's release.
Adding to the pressure is the resignation of Calley Means, MAHA's top ally and senior adviser to Kennedy, on Thursday. While Means didn't cite the reasons for leaving, saying he has "tremendous respect" for President Donald Trump and Kennedy, Politico reported that the stonewalled UPF definition was a "breaking point."
READ MORE: RFK Jr. adviser Calley Means resigns amid growing MAHA discontent over lack of progress
Since becoming the nation's top health official, Kennedy has linked Americans' overconsumption of ultraprocessed foods to childhood obesity and said the U.S. could not "reverse America's chronic disease epidemic without transforming our food system."
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. participates in a "Make America Healthy Again" summit in Washington, D.C., in September. Photo by Nathan Howard/Reuters
The Department of Health and Human Services and U.S. Department of Agriculture took an incremental step toward this goal in August by submitting for final review a proposed definition of these foods, which range from sugary cereals and sodas to burgers and store-bought breads.
"If industry pressure can delay even this first step toward greater transparency, what does that tell us about the challenges of making meaningful improvements to our food supply?" said Ashley Gearhardt, a professor of psychology at the University of Michigan who signed the letter.
The move could lay the groundwork for consumers to make informed decisions on ultraprocessed foods, which accounts for more than 70% of the packaged food supply in the U.S., according to one study.
Ultraprocessed foods are cheap, convenient and readily available, but numerous studies have linked them to negative health outcomes like cardiovascular disease, obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
Experts told PBS News that establishing a clear, structured definition is key to developing effective policy that aims to reduce people's consumption of ultraprocessed foods and improve public health.
Where did the term 'ultraprocessed foods' come from?
The term "ultraprocessed foods" comes from the NOVA classification system. Proposed in 2009 by researchers in Brazil, the NOVA system categorizes food and drinks into four different levels based on the amount of industrial processing a product undergoes after it's removed from nature and before it's prepared for meals and consumed.
Under the NOVA system, foods in the ultraprocessed category are those that have undergone "extensive industrial manipulation," said Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition epidemiologist and professor at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who also signed the letter to OMB. These foods "have been broken down and then reassembled using cosmetic additives like added colors, added flavors, emulsifiers, or things that make the texture more palatable to people," she added.
Many ultraprocessed food products are "barely even food" and "not designed for nourishment," said Gearhardt. Instead, she said they are designed for consumers "to finish the whole bag before you even realize it."
Watch the clip in the player above.
Kennedy told lawmakers at his confirmation hearings last year that ultraprocessed foods are a threat to children's health and "making them sick." Roughly three-quarters of infant and toddler foods are considered ultraprocessed, according to a February study published in Nutrients.
Ultraprocessed foods are often sugary, salty and fatty, and packaged for long shelf lives and portability, Taillie said.
The other three groups in the NOVA system are:
Fresh or minimally processed foods. That includes unprocessed fruit, seeds, eggs and plain meat, and minimally processed foods such as fruit that's been dried, squeezed, chilled or frozen.
Culinary ingredients. Think butter, sugar, honey, among other substances that have been extracted from whole foods for cooking.
Processed foods. These are products that have experienced some level of processing or preservation, including canned vegetables, cheese, salted nuts and smoked meats.

MIAMI (AP) — Vance became a hurricane Friday and the National Hurricane Center said it would strengthen rapidly as it nears Mexico's Pacific Coast.
Track the path of Hurricane Vance below.
Vance was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph (150 kph) as it churned about 455 miles (730 kilometers) south-southwest of Acapulco, and could become a major Category 3 hurricane before the end of Friday, the center said.
It was moving toward the north-northwest near 5 mph (8 kph), and this motion is expected to continue through the weekend, approaching the Puerto Vallarta area by Monday. The hurricane's outer bands were already funneling gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico's Gulf of Tehuantepec, the center said.
Grow your mind

It's been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean, with storms spawning in assembly-line fashion near Hawaii and Mexico as El Niño conditions worsened by global warming create unusual weather, like this week's severe flooding and tornadoes hitting the southwestern United States and the prolonged drought in Central America's Dry Corridor.
Vance would be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy. The World Meteorological Organization's Hurricane Committee doesn't use less common names beginning with Q, U, X, Y and Z.

Rollins says USDA is 'full-bore ahead' on Forest Service reorganization
Politics
Oct 23, 2026 7:52 PM EDT
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday that the Trump administration remains "full-bore ahead" with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service and other agencies after a judge blocked the changes last week.
WATCH: U.S. Forest Service cuts raise concerns on protecting public lands and fighting wildfires
The administration wants to move Forest Service headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City, shutter 23 research stations, and close many regional offices and replace them with state offices. It's part of a broader realignment at the Agriculture Department that also would change programs for food and nutrition, rural development and other services.
For now the plan is stalled under court order. But that's already under appeal, and Rollins made clear Thursday that the administration hasn't given up.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
"We are full-bore ahead in the reorganization," Rollins said during a conference call with reporters following an announcement on fertilizer production. "We believe in it more today than we ever have — taking the USDA to our constituents, which is rural America, the Forest Service out West."
Administration officials say the reorganization will trim costs and further concentrate resources in Western states that are home to nearly 90% of national forest lands.
Federal employee unions, environmental groups and local officials, including in California, Maryland and Washington state, are trying to quash the plan. They say the shuffling of employees is a ploy to achieve the administration's goal of deep cuts in the workforce.
U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria in California sided with those arguments in an Oct. 13 order halting the reorganization while a lawsuit from opponents works its way through the courts.
"If implemented, the planned reorganization activities will likely put thousands of USDA employees to the choice of relocating far from their current home — often to a different state — or losing their job," Chhabria wrote. He said the administration "almost certainly" violated congressional restrictions on using money on the reorganization that was intended for other purposes.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has been eliminating layers of management as part of President Donald Trump's push to slim the federal workforce and make it more efficient.
Trump also wants to take away one of the Forest Service's most prominent roles — fighting wildfires — and transfer responsibility to the new federal Wildland Fire Service. Congress so far has blocked that move.
With wildfires getting worse in recent decades due to climate change, battling them has consumed a greater share of the Forest Service budget. That's forced officials to look for cost savings elsewhere.
WATCH: Wildland firefighters feel increasing strain amid funding and staffing shortages
It's not clear how much the reorganization will actually save, said Chris Iverson, who spent almost three decades at the Forest Service before retiring from a leadership position during Trump's first term. Yet Iverson said the changes could result in the loss of personnel with extensive experience, including battling wildfires.
He added that the elimination of regional offices and creation of state offices could open the door to more influence by governors pushing the interests of the timber, oil and gas and grazing industries.
"It's just going to be a closer alignment of Forest Service leadership with state government priorities," Iverson said.
Gov. Spencer Cox in Utah has described the Forest Service reorganization, including a new headquarters in Salt Lake City, as "a big win for Utah and the West." GOP lawmakers said it would ensure agency officials get more local input.
The administration last month scaled back part of its plan and said 41 research facilities across the country that faced possible closure would remain open. Almost two dozen research stations still are slated to close.
The Forest Service workforce has been cut about 16% under Trump, from more than 39,000 employees to 33,000, according to government data.
During his first term, Trump moved the Bureau of Land Management to Colorado, citing many of the same reasons — including a desire to put top officials closer to the public lands they oversee. The Biden administration reversed course, moving BLM headquarters back to Washington, D.C., after two years.
The National Federation of Federal Employees union said a survey of Forest Service workers showed a large majority opposed the pending reorganization plan and most were unwilling to relocate.

Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election
World
Oct 23, 2026 7:31 PM EDT
KIRYAT SHMONA, Israel (AP) — Kiryat Shmona has long been a bastion of support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party. But that loyalty is no longer ironclad.
Once a bustling commercial center, Israel's northernmost city was temporarily evacuated three years ago after being battered by rockets from nearby Lebanon, and it still feels half-empty even though the attacks have mostly subsided. Although the town remains staunchly conservative, there are rumblings of displeasure with Netanyahu's handling of the latest war against the militant group Hezbollah, and that could bode poorly for him in Israel's election Tuesday.
READ MORE: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
Vowing to stop Hezbollah's attacks, Netanyahu led a bombing campaign in Lebanon and invaded the country twice since 2023. More than 4,000 Lebanese have been killed, and Israeli troops have occupied a swath of southern Lebanon, leveling multiple towns and displacing an estimated 1 million people.
Still, Hezbollah remains active. Some in Kiryat Shmona say Israel should have been even tougher; others say they no longer trust that Netanyahu cares about them.
Eti Ben Shabat, 64, says in previous elections she had always followed her family in voting for Likud, almost without thinking. But in recent years, she said, something snapped. She pointed in part to Netanyahu's broken promises to bring security to the north and dismantle Hezbollah.
"I don't want the lies to continue," she said.
In previous elections, support went heavy for Netanyahu
Netanyahu is unlikely to lose Kiryat Shmona entirely. But even a small dip in its support — and that of other traditional strongholds — could spell trouble for him.
It could tip a very tight election to the man aiming to replace him, Gadi Eisenkot. Or it could strengthen far-right parties, which would likely back Netanyahu to remain prime minister but would then have even greater power in a ruling coalition.
Kiryat Shmona has always supported right-wing parties, particularly Likud. In the last elections held in 2021 and 2022, around 50% of voters there chose Likud, compared to a quarter of voters nationwide, according to the Central Elections Committee.
"Kiryat Shmona, the way the city is socioeconomically and religion-wise, it is made for the right and specifically Likud," said Sami Malul, 72, a retired Likud city councilor who served as the town's acting mayor in 2008.
But the town is reeling from the war. The government evacuated Kiryat Shmona and dozens of other towns and villages along the Lebanese border for more than a year – from the time Hezbollah began firing on Israel after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel until a ceasefire with Hezbollah was reached in late 2024.
Netanyahu claimed to have subdued Hezbollah. So trust in him shattered among some in Kiryat Shmona when Hezbollah missiles again started hitting in March after Israel and the U.S. launched their war on Iran.
Israel's subsequent occupation of southern Lebanon has reduced but not stopped Hezbollah fire. Efforts by the Lebanese army to remove Hezbollah from southern Lebanon have made little progress.
Kiryat Shmona claims that nearly 80% of its 22,000 residents have returned, but locals say the real figure is closer to 50%. Streets feel empty and abandoned. On the main commercial drags, several shops remain shuttered. Others are open but devoid of customers.
Malul insists the government handled the war and the evacuation well, prioritizing residents' safety. He argued Kiryat Shmona has faced attacks since its founding and Netanyahu isn't to blame for the current situation.
Many others feel the same.
"We really love Bibi, and we can't choose anyone else, but he should see the needs of his people," said Maimon Amsalem, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Keeping our security is the most important thing, we don't want anything else."
For some, three years of war triggers a dramatic shift
Nissan Zeevi, a third-generation resident of northern Israel who lives in a town adjacent to Kiryat Shmona, has voted for Likud as long as he can remember. But this year he is running for a seat in parliament with the Beyachad opposition party, furious over what he calls Netanyahu's "abandonment of the north."
During the most recent war with Hezbollah, Zeevi founded Lobby 1701, an activist group advocating for better security in the north. He wants the Israeli military to increase its attacks against Hezbollah and maintain its buffer zone in southern Lebanon until the Lebanese government identifies Hezbollah as a terror organization.
"Residents in the north have been in a war for three years that hasn't ended," said Zeevi. "You can see the people's great frustration and great disappointment in Netanyahu."
"Netanyahu still has his base here, who will go with him through fire and water. But people have much more political awareness now," said Zeevi. "After 20 years, he needs to make way for new leadership."
In a small town, voting along family lines

Treasury proposes rule to curb high-tech investments in China and other adversaries
Politics
Oct 23, 2026 7:19 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other "countries of concern."
The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.
That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.
In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.
The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.
REAAD MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen
The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump's favored term for AI, "superintelligence" or SI.
The proposed rule "sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build," said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
The screening of outbound investments "recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can," Singleton said.
Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule "will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk."
Treasury's rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.
Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.
"It's just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program," said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.
In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.
Asked about Washington's proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that "Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one's interests."
She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.
Since Trump's first term, the United States and China — the world's two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They've restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China's rare earth minerals and America's advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other's products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.
But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

Seeking to help Collins in Maine, Trump exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs
Politics
Oct 23, 2026 6:48 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30.
The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.''
Collins, locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, issued a statement saying she'd spoken with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.''
WATCH: What Maine voters are saying about the Collins-Jackson Senate race
"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said.
She said she asked for tariff relief for such products "and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families."

Collins said she'd seek "additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner."
Trump started a trade war with America's longstanding ally and northern neighbor, reaching back to a Depression-era trade law to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. He charged that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly lashed back with tariffs of 15% to 50% on American products, matching Trump's import taxes dollar for dollar.
Trump ratcheted the dispute up from there last month by imposing a flat-out ban on $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.
The U.S. president has claimed that foreign countries pay his tariffs. In fact, U.S. importers do. And they often face the tough choice of having to pass along the higher costs to their customers or absorb them.
As the Nov. 3 midterm elections approach, many Americans are furious about the cost of living. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll of 2,140 U.S. adults, conducted Sept. 24-28, found that 65% now blame Trump's policies for persistently high prices more than factors outside of his control, signaling weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and unhappiness with the war with Iran, which has driven up the price of gasoline.
Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement, "Trump's desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies."
Collins complained that Trump's levies were hurting Maine farms and businesses that rely on Canadian imports when U.S.-made alternatives are not available. Her office cited the example of Maine wild blueberry growers who need specialized harvesting boxes from Canada that work with their processing equipment.

Defense attorneys in case over Charlie Kirk's killing say they need years to prepare for trial
Nation
Updated on Oct 24, 2026 8:55 AM EDT — Published on
Oct 23, 2026 6:03 PM EDT
Defense attorneys for the Utah man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk said they need several years to prepare their case and suggested a 2029 trial date.
An attorney for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, called the proposal "absurd" and accused defendant Tyler Robinson of trying to delay.
READ MORE: Utah judge decides Tyler Robinson will stand trial over Charlie Kirk's killing
Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf had been expected to set the trial date during a Friday hearing. However, no date was set and Graf scheduled the next hearing for Nov. 9.
Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in last year's killing of Kirk as the 31-year-old activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University. The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting, and his lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk's death.
He could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted.
Kirk helped galvanize youth voters around President Donald Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the case in a social media post prior to Friday's hearing. He said it should be tried "within a month." Trump criticized Graf — a former prosecutor appointed as a judge last year — for "taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to."
Utah County prosecutors allege the 23-year-old defendant targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with "Hey Facist! CATCH!" and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."
Prosecutors said they anticipate a 17-week trial and would be ready by October 2027. But rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed the trial begin in January 2028.
Erika Kirk's attorney said the trial should start next October. Dragging it out for years would violate her speedy trial rights under Utah law as a victim, said attorney Jeffrey Neiman.
"Under the Defendants' proposed schedule, Mr. Kirk's two children, who were one and three at the time he was murdered, will be six and eight years old by the time the trial concludes," Neiman wrote in a court filing. "They will face the uncertainty of this criminal proceeding longer than they had their father in their lives."
Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan extensive investigations into Robinson's life in a search for mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and to devote "substantial time" to issues such as jury selection.

President Donald Trump brushed off questions Friday about the role Elon Musk played in disruptions to service between the satellite system he owns and the drones Ukraine uses to fight Russia.
Watch Trump's remarks in the video player above.
"Elon will never do anything wrong," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "I know him very well. He's a fair person."
READ MORE: Trump administration offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that service remained slow from Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service. The disruption produced speed restrictions on Ukrainian drones, which have been unable to intercept Russia's jet-powered drones.
Trump said he hadn't heard that there are still problems with the service, and declined to comment on who ordered the restrictions to Starshield, telling a reporter, "I wouldn't tell you if I did know."
